taxonomy.source: Kew Plants of the World Online

project_inclusion.native_status_note: Kew treats the native range as Mexico through tropical America and Texas as introduced. That does not exclude it during the current local-occurrence-first phase.
project_inclusion.local_relevance_note: High-value Central Texas comparison species because it overlaps strongly in leaf shape with other morning glories and has already been part of the user's recent field-ID work.

morphology_keys.life_cycle: Annual in Flora of North America treatment.
morphology_keys.leaf_morphology: Leaf blades orbiculate to broadly ovate or 3–7-lobed, usually 20–80 mm long, with a cordate base. Surfaces glabrous or sparsely pilose.
morphology_keys.peduncle: Generally glabrous; can bear one to several flowers.
morphology_keys.sepals: Short, usually about 6–7 mm long; narrowly elliptic-oblong, lanceolate, or oblong; apex acute to obtuse, often mucronulate-caudate; margins ciliate.
morphology_keys.corolla: Small lavender to pink/purple funnel-shaped corolla, usually about 10–20 mm long in Flora of North America.
morphology_keys.fruit: Subglobose capsule; seed capsule view included in the curated photo set.
morphology_keys.flowering: Can flower over a long season in warm climates.

field_diagnostics.single_best_trait: Small flower + short sepals. Do not rely on the three-lobed leaf implied by the name.
fastest_traits: Leaves may be entire or deeply lobed

look_alikes.distinction: I. hederacea has much longer sepals, typically 12–24 mm, with an abruptly narrowed, long curved/spreading distal tip. I. triloba sepals are much shorter.
Leaf shape can overlap. Compare sepal form, corolla size, pubescence, and inflorescence architecture rather than leaf lobing alone.

field_diagnostics.comparison_upgrade: Against I. cordatotriloba, prioritize corolla + sepal scale together: FNA gives I. triloba corolla 10–20 mm and sepals 6–7 mm, versus I. cordatotriloba corolla 20–38 mm and sepals 8–14 mm. Leaf lobing overlaps and should not decide the ID.

ecology.habitat: Weedy/disturbed ground, sandy ground, moist pastures, clearings, thickets, roadsides, fence lines, and other open sites.
ecology.study_value: Excellent training species because the leaf can be misleading; the identification improves when sepal length and corolla size are prioritized.
